questions.q: Why does the lesson say a presentation's structure should differ from the written report's structure?
options: A presentation is linear and time-boxed, so it should lead with the question and headline finding rather than building up to a conclusion
Because technical audiences never ask questions during presentations
Because written reports are always shorter than presentations
Because presentations are not allowed to contain any data
questions.explain: The lesson explains that a report can be read at the reader's own pace and skipped around in, while a presentation's linear, time-boxed format calls for leading with the question and finding rather than the report's methods-first build-up.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend stating the hypothesis (slide 3) BEFORE showing any results?
options: Because hypothesis slides are required by presentation software templates
Because audiences cannot understand results without first seeing a hypothesis slide
It lets the audience judge results against the originally stated prediction, enforcing the same anti-HARKing discipline from Lesson 17
Because showing results first is technically impossible in slide format
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly connects this ordering to Lesson 17's anti-HARKing point -- stating the hypothesis first, before results, prevents the appearance of reframing the prediction after seeing the outcome.

questions.q: What does the lesson say backup slides are for, and when are they shown?
options: Detail a technical audience might probe in Q&A (full run log, raw data, fit parameters) -- shown only if asked, not presented by default
Slides that replace the limitations section entirely
The most important slides, always presented first
Slides containing only the title and acknowledgments
questions.explain: The lesson defines backup slides as supporting detail (run log, raw data, diagnosis detail) kept in reserve for Q&A rather than part of the main timed presentation.

questions.q: In the worked presentation outline, why does the results slide show BOTH the original (confounded) and corrected 5-qubit comparisons, rather than only the clean corrected one?
options: Because the original run was actually the more accurate one
The confound-and-correction comparison is itself part of the finding, and hiding the original run would make the presentation less credible, not more polished
Because presentation software requires at least two data points per slide
Because showing only one result is against conference rules
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly states that omitting the original, confounded run would reduce credibility with a technical audience -- the full confound-and-correction story is treated as a strength, not something to hide.

questions.q: Which of these is listed as a common presentation mistake?
options: Preparing answers to anticipated hard technical questions in advance
Including a limitations slide with the same care as the results slide
Spending too much time on methods detail that belongs in backup slides, running out of time for results and limitations
Stating the hypothesis clearly before showing results
questions.explain: The lesson lists over-spending time on methods detail (which should be in backup slides) as a common mistake -- the other three options are good practices the lesson recommends, not mistakes.
